# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

This dissertation set out to answer whether Deep Gaussian Processes improve on single-layer GPs for real-world machine learning tasks, and if so, when and at what cost.

## Key Findings

DGPs outperform single-layer GPs only on non-stationary, compositional targets. On the Kin8nm robot kinematics benchmark, DSVGP-2L reduced RMSE by 10.7% over SVGP (0.0699 vs 0.0783) and improved NLPD from $-1.116$ to $-1.241$. The improvement makes sense theoretically as Kin8nm's target is a composition of trigonometric functions of joint angles. This is precisely the hierarchical non-linearity where learned intermediate representations add value. On the UCI credit card default benchmark, where the target surface is smoother and more monotonic, DGPs matched but did not exceed single-layer GP performance.

The GP family delivers substantially better native probability calibration than classical models. On the credit card classification task, GP models achieved ECE of 0.010-0.021, compared to 0.087–0.225 for random forest, XGBoost, and logistic regression, a 4–22$\times$ improvement with no post-hoc calibration required. This held across all training set sizes from 425 observations onward. For regulatory applications under Basel IRB, where PD estimates must track observed default frequencies across rating grades, this property is significant as XGBoost's miscalibration would likely require post-hoc recalibration, while GP models' native calibration reduces this burden, but full compliance goes beyond just calibration metrics.

DSVGP-3L consistently fails to justify its extra compute costs. Across both datasets and all training scales, three-layer DGPs never meaningfully outperformed two-layer variants on any metric. At small training set sizes ($N \leq 500$), DSVGP-3L failed completely with $R^2 = 0.002$ on Kin8nm small scale and ROC-AUC = 0.523 on UCI small scale. They recovered fully by medium scale. At full scale, the extra layer added approximately $3.6$–$4\times$ training time and gave negligible gains. DSVGP-2L is therefore the more defensible deep configuration and achieves the benefits of depth when they exist, without the instability and cost of deeper architectures. 

The three-layer collapse observed here may be linked to the constant-mean hidden-layer architecture we used. Linear-mean ("skip-connected") variants [@salimbeni_doubly_2017] have evidence showing they may somewhat mitigate this, but were not tested. Three-layer DGPs may also prove to be more beneficial on very non-stationary targets at larger scales, but there was no evidence of this on the datasets tested here.

The right level of model complexity is determined by the structure of the target function, not by theoretical expressiveness alone. DGPs add genuine value when the problem demands it, but without non-stationarity and compositional target structures, single-layer GPs appear preferable.

## Limitations

These findings have several limitations. First, all experiments were conducted on CPU (Apple M2) without GPU acceleration. Absolute training times would be considerably shorter on modern hardware, though relative ratios between models should remain roughly similar. Second, only two datasets were evaluated, and so a broader benchmark across more domains and datasets would be needed to establish any generalisation claims. Third, the DGP architectures tested use fixed-width hidden layers and variable-width or residual DGP architectures [@salimbeni_doubly_2017] were not explored. Finally, the regulatory compliance claims are illustrative rather than definitive. Real-world PD model validation involves back-testing, portfolio-level stability testing, and model documentation requirements that extend well beyond the metrics evaluated here.

## Future Directions

There are several directions for future work. Stochastic-depth DGPs, analogous to stochastic depth in deep neural networks, where layers are skipped randomly during training, may address the small-data collapse of deep architectures. On the application side, regulatory back-testing of GP-based PD models, and evaluating stability of calibration across economic cycles and portfolio segments, would provide stronger evidence for or against adoption of GPs in practice.
